claims.claim: Medical terminology is the specialized vocabulary healthcare professionals use to name body structures, conditions, and treatments, and most of its terms are assembled from word parts — prefixes, word roots, suffixes, and combining vowels.
The key to understanding an unfamiliar medical term is recognizing its components (prefixes, roots, and suffixes), not memorizing the whole term.
Knowing the meaning of a small number of word parts helps with interpreting a large number of medical terms, because the same components recur across terms.
Common word roots carry core meanings: cardi(o)- heart, gastr(o)- stomach, neur(o)- nerve, derm(ato)- skin, hepat(o)- liver, nephr(o)- kidney.
Common prefixes and suffixes include hypo- (deficient, low), hyper- (excessive, high), -itis (inflammation), -ectomy (excision, removal by cutting), and -algia (pain).
When a word root is combined with a combining vowel (usually -o-), the result is a combining form (e.g., gastr/o), and terms are built by joining these parts.
Terms can be translated literally by joining the meanings of their parts — for example, osteoarthritis is inflammation of bone and joint (oste/o + arthr/o + -itis).
Hypothermia is low body temperature, usually below 95 degrees Fahrenheit; the word reads literally as low heat (hypo- + therm-).
Standardized terminology exists to make professional communication precise, reducing the risk of dangerous mix-ups — for example, confusing hypo- with hyper- reverses the meaning of a term.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether medical terminology is best framed as a patient-facing communication problem or as a professional precision tool.
positions: The NLM Understanding Medical Words tutorial frames learning word parts as closing the language gap between patients and professionals.
Clinical references such as the Merck Manual frame word parts as the way professionals decode terms precisely.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both honestly: terminology is a shared professional code whose fixed meanings create precision (the safety argument), and its parts are learnable, which is exactly the NLM tutorial's premise. No statistic about error rates is claimed.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Hypo- is glossed as 'deficient, low' in the Merck Manual, while some other references also use hypo- for anatomical location ('below').
positions: Merck Manual word-part glossary: hypo = deficient, low; hyper = excessive, high.
Some glossaries extend hypo- to 'below, under' for location terms (e.g., hypodermic).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses only the Merck Manual meanings (low/deficient vs high/excessive) and applies them to temperature and blood-sugar terms, avoiding anatomical-location uses.
